q: Audibility means the ability to be heard or capability of detecting sounds in certain range of frequencies.
e: True. Stiffer media generally carry it faster. Human audibility runs about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz. Below that is infrasound; above is ultrasound.

q: The range of frequencies a person can hear is known as the range of audibility.
e: True. Amplitude and loudness are separate ideas. Range of audibility is the frequency band a person can hear, about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz. Below 20 Hz is infrasound; above 20 000 Hz is ultrasound.

q: For humans with normal hearing, the lower limit is 20 Hz and the upper limit is about 20 000 Hz.
e: True. A different driver in place of humans would describe a different law. humans and normal have to stay with the same process.

q: For humans with normal hearing, the lower limit is 200 Hz and the upper limit is about 20 000 Hz.
e: False. Normal human hearing starts near 20 Hz, not 200 Hz, and runs to about 20 000 Hz. 200 Hz is already a spoken-word pitch. The true lower limit is an order of magnitude deeper.

q: Low frequency sounds which are under the lower limit of audibility (20 Hz) are called infrasound and cannot be heard by human.
e: True. Infrasound is sound below 20 Hz, inaudible as a tone, with long wavelengths that travel far. Ultrasound is the high-frequency opposite. Most echolocation and medical sonar are ultrasound, not infrasound.

q: Low frequency sounds which are under the lower limit of audibility (20 Hz) are called ultrasound and cannot be heard by human.
e: False. Sound under 20 Hz is infrasound. Ultrasound is the high-frequency side above about 20 000 Hz. Swap those names and medical imaging and earthquake rumbles trade places.

q: A vibrating ruler can be seen but not heard its vibrating sound.

q: High frequency sounds which are above the upper limit of audibility (20 000 Hz) are called ultrasound which cannot be heard by human ear.
e: True. Infrasound is the low-frequency counterpart. Ultrasound is sound above about 20 000 Hz, too high for the human ear. Short wavelength gives sharp echoes for imaging and ranging.

q: Bats and whales use ultrasound in echolocation and most sonar technologies use ultrasound.
e: True. Sonar is sound navigation and ranging: shout, time the echo, get distance. v = 2d/t is the go-and-return formula. Radar does the same job with radio waves.

q: Bats and whales use infrasound in echolocation and most sonar technologies use infrasound.
e: False. Bats, whales, and most sonar use ultrasound, whose short wavelength gives sharp echoes. Infrasound is the long-wave, low-frequency band. Navigation clicks are not infrasonic.
